content: 1. Individuals who are not currently employed but have actively sought employment and are available to accept a job opportunity are considered unemployed. This category also includes new graduates who are not engaged in any activity. For unemployed individuals, their occupation refers to the last job they held for which they are qualified. If information about the last job held is unavailable, the occupation in which the job seeker is seeking work can be used as a reference. 2. The ratio of unfilled posts to the total number of posts is an important indicator. The numerator represents the number of funded full-time positions that have remained vacant for at least six months and for which employers are actively recruiting. The denominator is the total number of funded full-time positions, both filled and unfilled. This ratio can be disaggregated by occupation and subnational level to provide a clearer understanding of workforce gaps. 3. The number of standard working hours per week, as defined by national laws or standards, is a key metric. This indicator should be reported at the national level and, if applicable, disaggregated by occupation when regulations on standard working hours vary across different professions. 4. The percentage of employed health workers with part-time contracts is another critical measure. The numerator is the number of active health workers with employment contracts below the national standard working hours, defined in headcounts. The denominator is the total number of active health workers, also defined in headcounts. This ratio can be further disaggregated by occupation and facility ownership. 5. The existence of national or subnational policies or laws regulating working hours and conditions is assessed through specific questions. These include whether the government has regulated the maximum number of working days per week, premiums for night work or overtime, and restrictions on night, overtime, or holiday work. It also examines whether there are provisions for paid annual leave based on tenure and whether regulations differ by employment status. 6. The existence of national or subnational policies or laws regulating minimum wage is evaluated. This indicator determines whether health workers are eligible to receive a minimum wage according to national or subnational laws. 7. The existence of national or subnational policies or laws regulating social protection is assessed through questions about maternity leave, parental leave, childcare support, leave entitlements for caring for sick family members, and leave for in-service training or continuing professional development. 8. The percentage of active health workers who are self-employed is an important labor market characteristic. The numerator is the number of self-employed health workers, defined in headcounts, while the denominator is the total number of active health workers, also defined in headcounts. This measure can be disaggregated by occupation. 9. The existence of national or subnational policies or laws regulating dual practice is evaluated. This includes whether health workers are allowed to engage in private practice in separate private environments, private wards or clinics associated with public facilities, or private services offered within public facilities but outside public service hours. 10. The existence of national or subnational policies or laws regulating compulsory service is assessed. This includes whether there are state employment programs for health workers, compulsory service with incentives, or compulsory service without incentives. 11. Measures to prevent attacks on health workers are evaluated through questions about governmental actions to reduce workplace violence. This includes whether reducing workplace violence is part of national policies, whether all stakeholders are involved in such policies, whether labor laws have been revised to address workplace violence, and whether data on workplace violence is collected and analyzed. 12. The number of attacks on the health-care system in the past 12 months is tracked. This includes attacks on facilities, health-care providers, transport, and patients. Both physical and psychological attacks are considered, including verbal abuse, bullying, harassment, and threats. 13. Total expenditure on the health workforce is a key economic indicator. This includes all resources dedicated to the health workforce, disaggregated by facility ownership. Data sources may include income tax records and Ministry of Health records. 14. The percentage of public expenditure on the compensation of health workers is another critical measure. This includes entry-level wages and salaries, as well as policies on public sector wage ceilings. 15. The gender wage gap in health workforce remuneration is addressed as part of efforts to promote decent work for all. This indicator highlights disparities in wages between male and female health workers and provides insights into gender equity in the health sector.
